tagline: Register an OAuth app in minutes, no approval - but GitHub nudges you toward GitHub Apps instead.
summary: GitHub OAuth apps are self-serve: register in Developer settings and you immediately get a client ID and secret, with no review or approval step for the app itself. The real decision is OAuth app vs GitHub App - GitHub's own docs recommend a GitHub App for most new integrations because OAuth apps can only act on behalf of a user and use coarse scopes.

difficulty.label: Very easy
difficulty.rationale: Self-serve registration with instant credentials and no approval gate for a standard OAuth app that lets users authorize access to their own GitHub data.

timeToFirstToken: About 10-15 minutes: register the app, set the callback URL, exchange a code for a token.

approvalWait.label: None for the OAuth app itself
approvalWait.detail: No verification or approval is required to create and use an OAuth app. A review only enters the picture if you later want a GitHub Marketplace listing, which is optional.

steps.title: Open Developer settings
steps.detail: Profile picture -> Settings -> Developer settings -> OAuth apps -> New OAuth App (verified path in GitHub's docs).

steps.title: Fill in registration fields
steps.detail: Application name, Homepage URL, optional description, and the Authorization callback URL (up to 10 callback URLs allowed). Keep everything public-safe - GitHub warns the data you enter is visible to users.

steps.title: Register and collect credentials
steps.detail: Click Register application. You get the client ID immediately and can generate a client secret. Store the secret in your secret manager, never in the repo.

steps.title: Decide OAuth app vs GitHub App
steps.detail: If you need fine-grained repository permissions, installation tokens, or to act as the app itself, build a GitHub App instead. GitHub explicitly recommends this for new work.

steps.title: Implement the authorize + token exchange
steps.detail: Redirect users to github.com/login/oauth/authorize with your client_id and scopes, then exchange the returned code for an access token server-side. Token expiry is enabled by default for new apps.

requirements: A GitHub account (or an organization you administer) - human step.
A public homepage URL and an HTTPS callback URL for production.
A decision on scopes: OAuth app scopes are coarse (e.g. repo, read:user); check whether a GitHub App's fine-grained permissions fit better.
nuances: GitHub's docs steer new integrations toward GitHub Apps: OAuth apps can only act on behalf of a user, use coarse scopes, and lack short-lived installation tokens.
A user or organization can own at most 100 OAuth apps.
Expire-user-access-tokens is on by default for newly registered apps - your code must handle refresh tokens.
Listing on the GitHub Marketplace is a separate, optional review; the OAuth app itself needs no approval.
Fine-grained permission needs (single-repo access) are a signal you picked the wrong app type, not a blocker.
agentCanDo: Read the current docs and produce the exact registration field values and authorize URL for your use case.
Compare OAuth app vs GitHub App for your feature list and recommend one.
Generate the token-exchange code in your stack.
humanMustDo: Create the OAuth app inside your GitHub account or org (requires your login and ownership).
Hold the client secret and accept GitHub's terms.
Choose and justify the scopes your users will see on the consent screen.

evidence.claim: OAuth apps are created under personal account or org Developer settings via a New OAuth App form with name, homepage URL, and up to 10 callback URLs; registration is a single form submit.

GitHub recommends building a GitHub App instead of an OAuth app for most cases: GitHub Apps offer fine-grained permissions, more user control, and short-lived tokens, while OAuth apps can only act on behalf of a user.
A user or organization can own up to 100 OAuth apps.
Expire user access tokens is enabled by default on new OAuth apps.
The registration path (Settings -> Developer settings -> OAuth apps) was verified in the docs on 2026-10-28; no app was actually created on a live account for this guide.

uncertainties: GitHub Marketplace listing requirements and review duration were not researched - only the OAuth-app creation path.
Docs pages are partly JS-rendered; the text capture used the published doc content as of 2026-10-28.
